about: What to do about a leaked credential, per vendor, from that vendor's own documentation. Each entry carries its source and how well it was verified; the browser view shows the steps on a finding's card. Anything not confirmed in a vendor's docs is marked and worded as uncertain rather than asserted.
universal: Deleting the transcript does not undo this: the value was already sent to the model vendor as chat context, and may be in their server-side logs.
Revoke first, then issue a replacement. If downtime matters, create the replacement, move your app to it, and revoke the old one immediately after.

live_credential.headline: This credential exists on this machine and appears in AI assistant history, so treat it as known to someone else.
steps: Revoke it wherever it was issued, then create a replacement.
Update every place that used it — the copy still on disk is listed on this card.
Check the service's audit or usage log for activity you do not recognise.

pattern.headline: This is a credential in a known vendor format found in AI assistant history.
steps: Confirm it is yours and still valid — the masked value here is enough to find it.
Revoke it at the vendor and issue a replacement.
Check the vendor's audit or usage log for activity you do not recognise.

configuration.headline: This secret sits in plain text in an AI tool's configuration file. It is not necessarily sent to a model, but anyone who can read the file can use it.
steps: Move it out of the configuration file into your environment or a secrets manager, if the tool supports that.
If the file has been shared, synced or backed up, revoke and replace the value as well.

session_cookie.headline: A session cookie is a live sign-in. Rotating it means ending the session, not changing a key.
steps: Sign out of all sessions for that account in its security settings; that invalidates the cookie.
Change the account password if you cannot end sessions individually.
Turn on two-factor authentication if it is not on already.

private_key.headline: A private key cannot be rotated in place: it has to be replaced everywhere it is trusted.
steps: Generate a new key pair.
Add the new public key everywhere the old one was trusted (servers, Git hosts, CI).
Remove the old public key from each of those places.
Delete the exposed private key file once nothing uses it.

prompt.headline: A password-like string was typed into an AI assistant.
steps: If it is a real password, change it on that service.
If the account supports it, sign out of other sessions and turn on two-factor authentication.

entropy.headline: A random-looking token near a secret-related word. Only the deep scan found it, and it may be nothing.
steps: Look at the value and decide whether it is a credential of yours.
If it is, revoke and replace it at whichever service issued it.
On the API keys page, open the key's ⋯ menu and choose Rotate key.
Pick when the old key expires: now, or after a grace period of up to seven days while you migrate.
Copy the new key — it is shown only once — and update your integration.
Watch the request logs until the old key has no traffic, then expire it.
notes: Dashboard rotation gives an overlap window, so rotating need not break production.
sk_live_ and rk_live_ are secret; pk_live_ is publishable and safe to expose.
Stripe says it monitors for exposed keys and may invalidate a leaked one itself.

steps: Invalidate the token immediately with the auth.revoke API call.
For a bot or user token, reinstall the app from OAuth & Permissions to mint a replacement.
For an app-level token, revoke and regenerate it under Basic Information → App-Level Tokens.
For an incoming webhook, delete that webhook URL in the app's settings and add a new one.
notes: xoxb- is a bot token, xoxp- a user token, xapp- an app-level token; a webhook is a secret URL, not a token.
Revoking a bot token deactivates it but does not uninstall the app.
Not confirmed in Slack's docs: whether one webhook can be revoked without affecting the others.

steps: Open Settings → API Keys and delete the exposed key; it starts returning 401 at once.
Create a replacement with the narrowest permission level that works, and copy it immediately.
Update your application configuration.
Check the email activity feed for sends you do not recognise.
notes: Keys start with "SG." and are shown only once.
SendGrid says it may delete an exposed key itself within moments of detecting it, which breaks the integration without warning.

steps: For an API key: open it and choose Delete this key, then create a replacement.
For the Auth Token, do it in stages: create a secondary token, move your integrations to it, then promote it to primary.
Check Monitor → Events for calls from addresses you do not recognise.
notes: Rotating the primary Auth Token directly breaks every integration at once; the secondary-token promotion exists to avoid that.
Each change emails the account's owners and admins.
Twilio does not document a prefix for API keys.

steps: Open Settings → Connections → Develop or manage connections and find the integration.
For an internal integration choose Refresh, which issues a new secret and invalidates the old one at once; for a personal access token, revoke it.
Update the secret everywhere it is used.
notes: New tokens start with ntn_; tokens issued before September 2024 start with secret_ and still work.
The audit log is Enterprise-only and only covers events since that plan started.

steps: Open Settings → Account → Security & Access and revoke the key; it stops working immediately.
Create a replacement and update whatever used it.
For an OAuth app, rotate the client secret, or revoke a single user token through the OAuth revoke endpoint.
notes: Admins can always manage keys; members only when an admin has enabled member API keys.
The audit log covers the last 90 days and is visible to workspace owners.

steps: For an API token, open its ⋯ menu and choose Roll: the old token stops working and the new one keeps the same permissions.
For the Global API Key, use Change in the API Keys section — but prefer replacing it with a scoped token.
Check the audit log for changes you did not make.
notes: Cloudflare recommends scoped tokens over the Global API Key, which has unscoped access to everything with no expiry.
The audit log records writes, not reads, and is available on every plan.

steps: On the Tokens page, use the token's menu to delete or regenerate it.
Copy the new secret immediately — it is shown only once — and update your integrations.
Check Settings → Security → Security History for token activity you do not recognise.
notes: A token's scope cannot be changed after creation; only renamed, regenerated or deleted.
Spaces access keys are a separate credential, rotated separately.
DigitalOcean revokes tokens it finds exposed in public GitHub repositories.

steps: Open the account tokens page, find the token and revoke it; revocation is immediate.
Create a replacement with the narrowest scope that works and an expiry, and copy it immediately.
Update your CI or local configuration.
notes: Tokens are shown only once, and project-scoped tokens cannot create new tokens.
Vercel revokes tokens it finds in public repositories, gists or npm packages.
The audit log is an Enterprise feature.

steps: On the API tokens page, revoke the token (or revoke all of them if you are unsure which leaked).
Create a replacement with an expiry, and scopes if you use scoped tokens; copy it immediately.
Update every integration that used it — revoking breaks all of them at once.
notes: A classic token carries the full access of the account that created it.
Atlassian revokes tokens it finds in public repositories.
Bitbucket's documentation mentions revocation taking up to ten minutes to propagate; whether that applies to every Atlassian token is not confirmed.

steps: Open the chat with @BotFather and send /mybots, or send /token.
Pick the bot and revoke the current token; BotFather issues a new one and the old one stops working at once.
Update the token wherever your bot runs.
notes: There is no web console and no request log for the Bot API: the token is the whole of the bot's security.
Only one token is active per bot at a time.

steps: Open your application → Bot and press Reset Token, confirming with two-factor authentication if you have it on.
Copy the new token immediately and restart your bot with it.
For a webhook, delete it in Server Settings → Integrations → Webhooks and create a new one.
notes: Resetting invalidates the old token at once, with no grace period: running bots disconnect immediately.
Discord scans public GitHub content and invalidates leaked tokens itself.
The server audit log records webhook changes for 45 days; token resets are not logged there.
